'''''Euphorbia esula''''', commonly known as '''green spurge''' or '''leafy spurge''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> is a species of [[Euphorbia|spurge]] native to central and southern [[Europe]] (north to [[England]], the [[Netherlands]], and [[Germany]]), and eastward through most of [[Asia]] north of the [[Himalaya]] to [[Korea]] and eastern [[Siberia]]. It can also be found in some parts of [[Alaska]].<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date=2017-12-18}}</ref><ref name=flora>''Flora Europaea'': [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Euphorbia+&SPECIES_XREF=esula&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Euphorbia esula'']</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref>

==Description==
[[Image:Euphorbia esula bluete.jpeg|thumb|left|Detail of flowers and immature seeds]]
It is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] growing to 1-1.2 m tall, with several stems branched from the base. The stems are smooth, hairless, or slightly hairy. The [[leaf|leaves]] are small, lanceolate, 4-8.5 cm long and up to 1 cm broad, with a slightly wavy margin. The [[flower]]s are small, produced in [[umbel]]s with a basal pair of bright yellow-green petal-like [[bract]]s. Clusters of the bracts appear in late spring, while the actual flowers do not develop until early summer. All parts of the plant contain a toxic white milky sap.<ref name=blamey/><ref name=rhs>Huxley, A, ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}</ref>

It reproduces readily like by [[seed]]s that have a high [[germination]] rate and may remain viable in the soil for at least eight years.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lym|first=Rodney G.|date=1998|title=The Biology and Integrated Management of Leafy Spurge (Euphorbia esula) on North Dakota Rangeland|jstor=3988402|journal=Weed Technology|volume=12|issue=2|pages=367–373|doi=10.1017/S0890037X00043955|hdl=10365/3132|s2cid=82415055 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> The seed [[Capsule (fruit)|capsules]] open explosively, dispersing seed up to 5 m from the parent plant, and may be carried further by water and wildlife. Leafy spurge also spreads vegetatively from the [[root]] system, which is complex, reported to reach 8 m into the ground and 5 m across, and may have numerous buds.<ref name=nps>[https://web.archive.org/web/20000118173454/http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/eues1.htm U.S. National Park Service description]</ref><ref name=invasive>[https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/profile/leafy-spurge Species Profile - Leafy Spurge (''Euphorbia esula'')], National Invasive Species Information Center, [[United States National Agricultural Library|National Agricultural Library]]</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Selleck|first1=G. W.|last2=Coupland|first2=R. T.|last3=Frankton|first3=C.|date=1962-02-01|title=Leafy Spurge in Saskatchewan|journal=Ecological Monographs|volume=32|issue=1|pages=1–29|doi=10.2307/1942359|issn=1557-7015|jstor=1942359|hdl=10365/3208|url=https://library.ndsu.edu/ir/bitstream/10365/3208/1/620sel62.pdf|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

There are two [[subspecies]] and a [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] subspecies:<ref name=grin/><ref name=blamey/>
*''Euphorbia esula'' subsp. ''esula''. Leaves broadest near apex; umbel bracts 5–15 mm. Throughout the range of the species.
*''Euphorbia esula'' subsp. ''tommasiniana'' (Bertol.) Kuzmanov (syn. ''E. waldsteinii'' (Sojak) A.R.Smith; ''E. virgata'' Waldst. & Kit.). Leaves broadest at the middle; umbel bracts 12–35 mm. Eastern Europe, western Asia.
*''Euphorbia esula'' nothosubsp. ''pseudovirgata'' (Schur) Govaerts. Hybrid between the above two subspecies.

==Confusion with ''Euphorbia virgata''==
It has commonly been confused with ''[[Euphorbia virgata]]''. ''E. esula'' is no longer considered a permanent component of the North American flora.<ref name=fna>{{cite web |title=Euphorbia virgata |publisher=Flora of North America|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242321554 |access-date=2018-08-17}}</ref> ''E. esula'' is restricted to certain parts of Europe and not considered a weedy species, while ''E. virgata'' is found throughout the United States and Canada and has caused significant economic and ecological impacts.<ref name="fna"/> ''E. virgata'' is best distinguished from ''E. esula'' by its leaves, which are 6-15 times longer than wide with margins that are (near-)parallel at the middle of the blade, while ''E. esula'' leaves are wider toward the tip, usually 3-8 times longer than wide, with margins that are not parallel at the middle of the leaf. In addition, the apex of ''E. virgata'' is usually acute and the base is truncate to attenuate, while the apex of ''E. esula'' is rounded or subacute and the base is more gradually attenuate or cuneate.<ref name="fna"/> Mentions of ''E. esula'' in the North American flora and invasive species literature are now referred to ''E. virgata''.
